context.hint: A minimal repair made the shared cross-origin redirect predicate recognize the proxy-credential name case-insensitively. One-hop cross-origin tests now leak nothing, same-origin and relative redirects preserve credentials, mixed casing is stripped, and unrelated challenge and marker headers survive. The next question is whether a longer redirect chain re-injects the credential on a later hop, and whether default-port or relative-Location origin spellings cause under- or over-stripping.
context.surface: A dependency-free JavaScript HTTP client with a low-level request entry point, a fetch-style entry point, a shared redirect handler, a proxy-agent component, and disposable loopback HTTP servers.
assumptions: The observer can read and modify a disposable local source tree, run a JavaScript runtime, and start ephemeral loopback servers; no public target, production service, or installed dependency is used.
The attacker controls caller-supplied request header names and values and the destination of a redirect, but not the client source or the local fixture.
A proxy credential is a request header intended only for a proxy, while an ordinary authorization credential is intended for the origin; both must be removed when the redirect target changes origin.
The client source ships without installed development dependencies, so purpose-built local scripts are used; official benchmark evaluation is external and local logs are not an official pass.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: adding a case-insensitive proxy-credential name check to the shared cross-origin predicate removes all observed leaks without a second code path. Prerequisites: a disposable patched copy and the existing two-server fixture. Bounded test: patch the predicate, rerun the casing and array matrix for 302 and 307, then run a benign regression with a direct request, a relative same-origin redirect, a cross-origin redirect carrying mixed-case credentials plus a proxy challenge and duplicate marker header, and the fetch-style API. Expected supporting result: zero cross-origin credential deliveries, same-origin and direct requests preserved, challenge and marker headers preserved. Falsifier: any leak remains or any benign header is lost. Cleanup: keep the patch in the disposable copy and export only the diff.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: sanitized headers are not written back to the request state, so a later hop of a multi-hop chain re-sends the original credential. Prerequisites: patched copy and three loopback origins. Bounded test: A redirects to B, B redirects to C; send both credential families and a marker at A and inspect C with the low-level API and the fetch-style API. Expected supporting result: C receives neither credential and receives the marker. Falsifier: either credential reappears at C. Cleanup: close all listeners and retain the chain log.

Hypothesis: a relative Location can resolve to a different origin when the current origin uses an implicit default port, causing under-stripping. Prerequisites: a server on the default port and a second origin on a non-default port. Bounded test: send a credential and marker through a relative redirect on the default port, an explicit default-port absolute redirect, and a redirect to the other port. Expected supporting result: same-origin spellings preserve and the different port strips. Falsifier: a different port preserves or a same-origin spelling strips. Cleanup: close both servers.

Hypothesis: adding one more credential name to a length-sensitive predicate causes over-stripping of an unrelated header with a similar name or changes duplicate-header handling. Prerequisites: patched copy and a fixture with duplicate non-credential headers. Bounded test: send a relative same-origin redirect with a changed query, both credential families, a proxy challenge, and a duplicated marker header; record all final headers. Expected supporting result: credentials and duplicate marker survive, challenge survives. Falsifier: a benign header is dropped or merged unexpectedly. Cleanup: close the server and save the raw header log.

evaluations.rationale: The incumbent patch remains the best artifact and is the fallback, but it has no new check. It is rescored and deferred to the chain experiment, which tests a failure mode not covered by one-hop evidence.
Selected. Multi-hop re-injection is the most plausible way the one-hop repair could fail and is directly executable on the existing fixture. It also gives both APIs a shared expected header set.
Deferred, not refuted. The default-port and relative-Location control is strong but overlaps the selected chain action, so it is folded into the same run rather than repeated as a separate round.

Deferred, not refuted. Duplicate-header and challenge survival are useful over-strip controls and are folded into the selected robustness script, but they do not discriminate a state-persistence failure.

observation.summary: The patched client was exercised on a two-hop cross-origin chain (A to B to C). The low-level and fetch-style APIs both delivered the final request without either credential family and with the marker intact. A relative same-origin redirect with a changed query preserved both credentials and a duplicated non-credential header. A 303 changed the method, removed content-type, stripped both credentials, and kept the marker. A separate default-port test showed that relative and explicit default-port Locations preserved credentials while a different port stripped them. No later-hop re-injection or origin-spelling error was observed.
observation.next_hint: Verify the exported patch on a fresh pristine tree rather than the in-place development copy. Apply only the saved diff, confirm the changed-file scope, and rerun the canonical matrix and benign regression there before preparing the external evaluator handoff.
